mn38:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in the Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapindika’s Park.
mn38:2.1: Now on that occasion a pernicious view had arisen in a bhikkhu called Sāti, son of a fisherman; thus:
mn38:2.2: ‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).’
mn38:3.1: Many bhikkhus heard that this was so.
mn38:3.2: ‘It seems that this pernicious view has arisen in the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman:
mn38:3.3: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).”’
mn38:3.4: Then they went to the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman,[^1] and they asked him:
mn38:3.5: ‘Friend, is it true, as it seems, that the following pernicious view has arisen in you:
mn38:3.6: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths)”?’
mn38:3.7: ‘Exactly so, friends. As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).’
mn38:3.8: Then the bhikkhus desiring to detach him from that pernicious view, pressed and questioned and cross-questioned him thus:
mn38:3.9: ‘Friend Sāti, do not say thus, do not misrepresent the Blessed One, it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not speak thus,
mn38:3.10: for consciousness has been stated in many discourses by the Blessed One to be dependently-arisen, since without the condition (for it) consciousness has no positive being.’
mn38:3.11: Yet although pressed and questioned and cross-questioned by them in this way, the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, still obstinately misapprehended according to his pernicious view and insisted upon it, saying:
mn38:3.12: ‘Exactly so, friends, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).’
mn38:4.1: Since the bhikkhus were unable to detach him from that pernicious view, they went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, they sat down at one side. When they had done so, they said to the Blessed One:
mn38:4.2: ‘Venerable sir, this pernicious view has arisen in the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman:
mn38:4.3: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).”
mn38:4.4: We heard, venerable sir, that this pernicious view had arisen in the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman:
mn38:4.5: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).”
mn38:4.6: Then, venerable sir, we went to the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, and we said to him:
mn38:4.7: ‘Friend, is it true, as it seems, that the following pernicious view has arisen in you:
mn38:4.8: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths)”?’
mn38:4.9: When this was said, venerable sir, the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, said to us:
mn38:4.10: ‘Exactly so, friends. As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).’
mn38:4.11: Then, venerable sir, desiring to detach him from that pernicious view, we pressed and questioned and cross-questioned him thus:
mn38:4.12: ‘Friend Sāti, do not say thus, do not misrepresent the Blessed One, it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not speak thus,
mn38:4.13: for consciousness has been stated in many discourses by the Blessed One to be dependently-arisen, since without the condition (for it) consciousness has no positive being.’
mn38:4.14: Yet although pressed and questioned and cross-questioned by us in this way, venerable sir, the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, still obstinately misapprehended according to his pernicious view and insisted upon it, saying:
mn38:4.15: ‘Exactly so, friends, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).’
mn38:4.16: Since we have been unable to detach the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, from this pernicious view, venerable sir, we have reported this matter to the Blessed One.’
mn38:5.1: Then the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu thus:
mn38:5.2: ‘Come, bhikkhu, tell the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, in my name:
mn38:5.4: ‘Even so, venerable sir,’ he replied, and he went to the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, and told him:
mn38:5.6: ‘Even so, friend,’ he replied, and he went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, the Blessed One asked him:
mn38:5.7: ‘Sāti, is it true, as it seems, that the following pernicious view has arisen in you:
mn38:5.8: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths)”?’
mn38:5.9: ‘Exactly so, venerable sir. As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that travels and traverses (the round of rebirths).’
mn38:5.11: ‘Venerable sir, it is what speaks and feels and experiences here and there the ripening of good and evil actions.’
mn38:5.12: ‘Misguided man, whom have you ever heard me teach the Dhamma to in that way?
mn38:5.13: Misguided man, has not consciousness been stated by me in many discourses to be dependently-arisen, since without the condition (for it) consciousness has no positive being?
mn38:5.14: But you, misguided man, have both misrepresented us by your wrong grasp of it and worked your own undoing by storing up much demerit,
mn38:5.15: for this will be long for your harm and suffering.’
mn38:6.1: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:
mn38:6.3: has this bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, kindled (in himself) even a spark (of understanding) in this Dhamma and Discipline?’
mn38:6.6: When this was said, the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, sat silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping and head down, glum and with nothing to say.
mn38:6.7: Then knowing that, the Blessed One told the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman:
mn38:6.8: ‘Misguided man, you will be described by this your own pernicious view.
mn38:6.9: I shall question the bhikkhus on this matter.’
mn38:7.1: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus:
mn38:7.2: ‘Bhikkhus, do you know the Dhamma taught by me as this bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, does when he both misrepresents us by his wrong grasp (of it) and works his own undoing by storing up much demerit?’
mn38:7.4: for consciousness has been stated by the Blessed One in many discourses to be dependently-arisen, since without the condition (for it) consciousness has no positive being.’
mn38:7.6: that you know the Dhamma taught by me thus:
mn38:7.7: for consciousness has been stated by me in many discourses to be dependently-arisen, since without the condition (for it) consciousness has no positive being.’
mn38:7.8: But this misguided man, Sāti, son of a fisherman, both misrepresents us by his wrong grasp (of it) and works his own undoing by storing up much demerit:
mn38:7.9: for this will be long for his harm and suffering.’
mn38:8.1: ‘Bhikkhus, consciousness is reckoned only by the condition dependent on which it arises:
mn38:8.2: when consciousness arises dependent on eye and forms, it is reckoned only as eye-consciousness;
mn38:8.3: when consciousness arises dependent on ear and sounds, it is reckoned only as ear-consciousness;
mn38:8.4: when consciousness arises dependent on nose and odours, it is reckoned only as nose-consciousness;
mn38:8.5: when consciousness arises dependent on tongue and flavours, it is reckoned only as tongue-consciousness;
mn38:8.6: when consciousness arises dependent on body and tangibles, it is reckoned only as body-consciousness;
mn38:8.7: when consciousness arises dependent on mind and dhammas, it is reckoned only as mind-consciousness.
mn38:8.8: ‘Just as a fire is reckoned only by the condition dependent on which it burns:
mn38:8.9: when fire burns dependent on logs, it is reckoned only as a log fire;
mn38:8.10: when fire burns dependent on faggots, it is reckoned only as a faggot fire;
mn38:8.11: when fire burns dependent on grass, it is reckoned only as a grass fire;
mn38:8.12: when fire burns dependent on cowdung, it is reckoned only as a cowdung fire;
mn38:8.13: when fire burns dependent on chaff, it is reckoned only as a chaff fire;
mn38:8.14: when fire burns dependent on rubbish, it is reckoned only as a rubbish fire—
mn38:8.15: so too, bhikkhus, consciousness is reckonable only by the condition dependent on which it arises.
mn38:8.16: When consciousness arises dependent on eye and forms it is reckoned only as eye-consciousness;
mn38:8.17: when consciousness arises dependent on ear and sounds it is reckoned only as ear-consciousness;
mn38:8.18: when consciousness arises dependent on nose and odours it is reckoned only as nose-consciousness;
mn38:8.19: when consciousness arises dependent on tongue and flavours it is reckoned only as tongue-consciousness.
mn38:8.20: When consciousness arises dependent on body and tangibles it is reckoned only as body-consciousness.
mn38:8.21: When consciousness arises dependent on mind and dhammas it is reckoned only as mind-consciousness.
mn38:9.1: ‘“This (entity) is”: bhikkhus, is this how you see it?’
mn38:9.3: ‘“Its coming to positive being is due to its nutriment”: bhikkhus, is this how you see it?’
mn38:9.5: ‘“Whatever (the entity that) is, with the cessation of its nutriment it has the nature of cessation”: bhikkhus, is this how you see it?’
mn38:10.1: ‘“This (entity) is, is it not?”: bhikkhus, does uncertainty arise in one who doubts in that way?’
mn38:10.3: ‘“Is its coming to positive being due to its nutriment, or is it not?”: bhikkhus, does uncertainty arise in one who doubts in that way?’
mn38:10.5: ‘“Whatever (the entity that) is, with the cessation of its nutriment has it the nature to change, or has it not?”: bhikkhus, does uncertainty arise in one who doubts in that way?’
mn38:11.1: ‘“This (entity) is”: bhikkhus, is uncertainty abandoned in one who sees it thus as it actually is with right understanding?’
mn38:11.3: ‘“Its coming to positive being is due to its nutriment”: bhikkhus, is uncertainty abandoned in one who sees it thus as it actually is with right understanding?’
mn38:11.5: ‘“Whatever (the entity that) is, with the cessation of its nutriment it has the nature of cessation”: bhikkhus, is uncertainty abandoned in one who sees it thus as it actually is with right understanding?’
mn38:12.1: ‘“This (entity) is”: bhikkhus, are you such that you are free from uncertainty here?’
mn38:12.3: ‘“Its coming to positive being is due to its nutriment”: bhikkhus, are you such that you are free from uncertainty here?’
mn38:12.5: ‘“Whatever (the entity that) is, with the cessation of its nutriment it has the nature of cessation”: bhikkhus, are you such that you are free from uncertainty here?’
mn38:13.1: ‘“This (entity) is”: bhikkhus, is it well viewed thus as it actually is with right understanding?’
mn38:13.3: ‘“Its coming to positive being is due to its nutriment”: bhikkhus, is it well viewed thus as it actually is with right understanding?’
mn38:13.5: ‘“Whatever (the entity that) is, with the cessation of its nutriment it has the nature of cessation”: bhikkhus, is it well viewed thus as it actually is with right understanding?’
mn38:14.1: ‘Bhikkhus, purified and bright as this view is, were you to adhere to it, cherish it, treasure it, and call it your own, would you then understand the Dhamma that has been taught as similar to a raft[^2], being for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping?’
mn38:14.3: ‘Bhikkhus, purified and bright as this view is, were you not to adhere to it, cherish it, treasure it, and call it your own, would you then understand the Dhamma that has been taught as similar to a raft, being for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping?’
mn38:15.1: ‘Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of nutriment for the maintenance of creatures that already are (entities) and for the assistance of those seeking to renew positive being.
mn38:15.3: They are physical food as nutriment whether gross or subtle, contact as the second, volition about (the state of) mind as the third, and consciousness as the fourth.
mn38:16.1: ‘Now these four kinds of nutriment have what as their source, have what as their origin, what brings them birth, what provides them with being?
mn38:16.2: These four kinds of nutriment have craving as their source, have craving as their origin, craving brings them birth, craving provides them with being.
mn38:16.3: ‘And this craving has what as its source, has what as its origin, what brings it birth, what provides it with being?
mn38:16.4: Craving has feeling as its source, has feeling as its origin, feeling brings it birth, feeling provides it with being.
mn38:16.5: ‘And this feeling has what as its source, has what as its origin, what brings it birth, what provides it with being?
mn38:16.6: Feeling has contact as its source, has contact as its origin, contact brings it birth, contact provides it with being.
mn38:16.7: ‘And this contact has what as its source, has what as its origin, what brings it birth, what provides it with being?
mn38:16.8: Contact has the sixfold base as its source, has the sixfold base as its origin, the sixfold base brings it birth, the sixfold base provides it with being.
mn38:16.9: ‘And this sixfold base has what as its source, has what as its origin, what brings it birth, what provides it with being?
mn38:16.10: The sixfold base has name-and-form as its source, has name-and-form as its origin, name-and-form brings it birth, name-and-form provides it with being.
mn38:16.11: ‘And this name-and-form has what as its source, has what as its origin, what brings it birth, what provides it with being?
mn38:16.12: Name-and-form has consciousness as its source, has consciousness as its origin, consciousness brings it birth, consciousness provides it with being.
mn38:16.13: ‘And this consciousness has what as its source, has what as its origin, what brings it birth, what provides it with being?
mn38:16.14: Consciousness has formations as its source, has formations as its origin, formations bring it birth, formations provide it with being.
mn38:16.15: ‘And these formations have what as their source, have what as their origin, what brings them birth, what provides them with being?
mn38:16.16: Formations have ignorance as their source, have ignorance as their origin, ignorance brings them birth, ignorance provides them with being.
mn38:17.1: ‘So, bhikkhus, it is with ignorance as condition that formations come to be;
mn38:17.4: with name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base;
mn38:17.5: with the sixfold base as condition, contact;
mn38:17.11: it is with birth as condition that ageing and death come to be, and (also) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.
mn38:17.12: That is how there is an origin to this whole mass of suffering.
mn38:18.1: ‘“With birth as condition, ageing and death”: so it was said.
mn38:18.2: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:18.3: ‘With birth as condition, ageing and death, venerable sir:
mn38:18.4: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:18.5: with birth as condition, ageing and death.’
mn38:18.6: ‘“With being as condition, birth”: so it was said.
mn38:18.7: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:18.8: ‘With being as condition, birth, venerable sir:
mn38:18.9: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:18.11: ‘“With clinging as condition, being”: so it was said.
mn38:18.12: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:18.13: ‘With clinging as condition, being, venerable sir:
mn38:18.14: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:18.16: ‘“With craving as condition, clinging”: so it was said. Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:18.17: ‘With craving as condition, clinging, venerable sir:
mn38:18.18: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:18.20: ‘“With feeling as condition, craving”: so it was said.
mn38:18.21: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:18.22: ‘With feeling as condition, craving, venerable sir:
mn38:18.23: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:18.25: ‘“With contact as condition, feeling”: so it was said.
mn38:18.26: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:18.27: ‘With contact as condition, feeling, venerable sir:
mn38:18.28: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:18.30: ‘“With the sixfold base as condition, contact”: so it was said.
mn38:18.31: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:18.32: ‘With the sixfold base as condition, contact, venerable sir:
mn38:18.33: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:18.34: with the sixfold base as condition, contact.’
mn38:18.35: ‘“With name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base”: so it was said.
mn38:18.36: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:18.37: ‘With name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base, venerable sir:
mn38:18.38: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:18.39: with name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base.’
mn38:18.40: ‘“With consciousness as condition, name-and-form”: so it was said.
mn38:18.41: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:18.42: ‘With consciousness as condition, name-and-form, venerable sir:
mn38:18.43: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:18.45: ‘“With formations as condition, consciousness”: so it was said.
mn38:18.46: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:18.47: ‘With formations as condition, consciousness, venerable sir:
mn38:18.48: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:18.50: ‘“With ignorance as condition, formations”: so it was said.
mn38:18.51: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:18.52: ‘With ignorance as condition, formations, venerable sir:
mn38:18.53: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:19.2: So you say thus, and I also say thus:
mn38:19.3: “That is, when this is; that arises with the arising of this,” that is to say:
mn38:19.7: with name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base;
mn38:19.8: with the sixfold base as condition, contact;
mn38:19.14: it is with birth as condition that ageing and death come to be, and (also) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.
mn38:19.15: That is how there is an origin to this whole mass of suffering.’
mn38:20.1: ‘With the remainderless fading and ceasing of ignorance, cessation of formations;
mn38:20.2: with the cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness;
mn38:20.3: with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form;
mn38:20.4: with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the sixfold base;
mn38:20.5: with the cessation of the sixfold base, cessation of contact;
mn38:20.6: with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling;
mn38:20.7: with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving;
mn38:20.8: with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging;
mn38:20.9: with the cessation of clinging, cessation of being;
mn38:20.10: with the cessation of being, cessation of birth;
mn38:20.11: with the cessation of birth, ageing and death cease, and (also) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.
mn38:20.12: That is how there is a cessation to this whole mass of suffering.
mn38:21.1: ‘“With cessation of birth, cessation of ageing and death”: so it was said.
mn38:21.2: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:21.3: ‘With cessation of birth, cessation of ageing and death, venerable sir:
mn38:21.4: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:21.5: with cessation of birth, cessation of ageing and death.’

mn38:21.7: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:21.8: ‘With cessation of being, cessation of birth, venerable sir:
mn38:21.9: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:21.10: with cessation of being, cessation of birth.’

mn38:21.12: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:21.13: ‘With cessation of clinging, cessation of being, venerable sir:
mn38:21.14: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:21.15: with cessation of clinging, cessation of being.’
mn38:21.16: ‘“With cessation of craving, cessation of clinging”: so it was said.
mn38:21.17: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:21.18: ‘With cessation of craving, cessation of clinging, venerable sir:
mn38:21.19: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:21.20: with cessation of craving, cessation of clinging.’
mn38:21.21: ‘“With cessation of feeling, cessation of craving”: so it was said.
mn38:21.22: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:21.23: ‘With cessation of feeling, cessation of craving, venerable sir:
mn38:21.24: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:21.25: with cessation of feeling, cessation of craving.’
mn38:21.26: ‘“With cessation of contact, cessation of feeling”: so it was said.
mn38:21.27: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:21.28: ‘With cessation of contact, cessation of feeling, venerable sir:
mn38:21.29: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:21.30: with cessation of contact, cessation of feeling.’
mn38:21.31: ‘“With cessation of the sixfold base, cessation of contact”: so it was said.
mn38:21.32: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:21.33: ‘With cessation of the sixfold base, cessation of contact, venerable sir:
mn38:21.34: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:21.35: with cessation of the sixfold base, cessation of contact.’
mn38:21.36: ‘“With cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the sixfold base”: so it was said.
mn38:21.37: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:21.38: ‘With cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the sixfold base, venerable sir:
mn38:21.39: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:21.40: with cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the sixfold base.’
mn38:21.41: ‘“With cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form”: so it was said.
mn38:21.42: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:21.43: ‘With cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form, venerable sir:
mn38:21.44: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:21.45: with cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form.’
mn38:21.46: ‘“With cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness”: so it was said.
mn38:21.47: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:21.48: ‘With cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness, venerable sir:
mn38:21.49: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:21.50: with cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness.’
mn38:21.51: ‘“With cessation of ignorance, cessation of formations”: so it was said.
mn38:21.52: Now is that so, bhikkhus, or not, or how does it appear in this case?’
mn38:21.53: ‘With cessation of ignorance, cessation of formations, venerable sir:
mn38:21.54: so it appears to us in this case—
mn38:21.55: with cessation of ignorance, cessation of formations.’
mn38:22.2: So you say thus, and I also say thus:
mn38:22.3: “That is not, when this is not; that ceases with the cessation of this,” that is to say:
mn38:22.4: with cessation of ignorance, cessation of formations;
mn38:22.5: with cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness;
mn38:22.6: with cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form;
mn38:22.7: with cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the sixfold base;
mn38:22.8: with cessation of the sixfold base, cessation of contact;
mn38:22.9: with cessation of contact, cessation of feeling;
mn38:22.10: with cessation of feeling, cessation of craving;
mn38:22.11: with cessation of craving, cessation of clinging;
mn38:22.12: with cessation of clinging, cessation of being;
mn38:22.13: with cessation of being, cessation of birth;
mn38:22.14: with cessation of birth, ageing and death cease, and (also) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.
mn38:22.15: That is how there is a cessation to this whole mass of suffering.’
mn38:23.1: ‘Bhikkhus, knowing and seeing in this way, would you run back to the past thus:
mn38:23.2: “Were we in past time? Were we not in past time? What were we in past time? How were we in the past time? Having been what, what were we in the past time?”’
mn38:23.4: ‘Knowing and seeing in this way, would you run forward to the future thus—
mn38:23.5: “Shall we be in future time? Shall we not be in future time? What shall we be in future time? How shall we be in future time? Having been what, what shall we be in future time?”’
mn38:24.1: ‘Bhikkhus, knowing and seeing in this way, would you be doubtful about the present in yourselves now—
mn38:24.2: “Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? Whence has this creature come? Whither will it be bound?”’
mn38:24.4: ‘Bhikkhus, knowing and seeing in this way, would you speak thus—
mn38:24.5: “The Teacher is respected by us: we speak (as we do) out of respect for the Teacher”?’
mn38:24.7: ‘Knowing and seeing in this way, would you speak thus—
mn38:24.8: “A monk told us, and (other) monks (did too); but we do not speak thus”?’
mn38:24.10: ‘Knowing and seeing in this way, would you acknowledge another[^3]?’
mn38:24.12: ‘Knowing and seeing in this way would you return to the ordinary monks’ and divines’ duties, and to the good omens open to the tumult of debate,[^4] as having a core (of truth)?’
mn38:24.14: ‘Bhikkhus, is it not that you speak only of what you have yourselves known, seen and experienced?’
mn38:25.1: ‘Good, bhikkhus. So you have been guided by me with a Dhamma (with effect) visible here and now, not (after a lapse) of time, inviting inspection, onward-leading, and experienceable by the wise each of himself.
mn38:25.2: This Dhamma, bhikkhus, (has effect) visible here and now, not (after a lapse) of time, it invites inspection, is onward-leading, and is experienceable by the wise each of himself—
mn38:25.3: it was with reference to this that it has been said.’
mn38:26.1: ‘Bhikkhus, precipitation of an embryo (in a womb) comes about with the concurrence of three (things).
mn38:26.2: Here there is concurrence of the mother and the father, but it is not the mother’s season, and no creature to be reborn is ready, in which case there is no precipitation in the womb.
mn38:26.3: Here there is concurrence of the mother and the father, and it is the mother’s season, but no creature to be reborn is ready, in which case there is no precipitation in the womb.
mn38:26.4: But owing to the fact that there is concurrence of the mother and the father, and it is the mother’s season, and a creature to be reborn is ready, there thus comes about precipitation of an embryo (in a womb) with the concurrence of three (things).
mn38:27.1: ‘The mother then carries the embryo in the womb for nine or ten months, with much anxiety as a great burden.
mn38:27.2: Then at the end of nine or ten months the mother gives birth with much anxiety as a great burden.
mn38:27.3: Then when it is born, she nourishes it with her own blood,
mn38:27.4: for the mother’s breast-milk is called blood in the Noble Ones’ Discipline.
mn38:28.1: ‘Necessitated by his growth and necessitated by the maturing of his faculties,
mn38:28.2: the child plays with such childish games as a toy plough, ‘tipcat’, turning somersaults, a toy windmill, a toy measure, a toy car, a toy bow and arrow.
mn38:29.1: ‘Necessitated by his growth and necessitated by the maturing of his faculties,
mn38:29.2: the youth becomes furnished and invested with the five cords of sensual desire, he enjoys them, namely:
mn38:29.3: forms cognizable through the eye that are wished-for, desired, agreeable, and pleasing, connected with sensual desire and provocative of lust;
mn38:29.7: tangibles cognizable through the body that are wished-for, desired, agreeable, and pleasing, connected with sensual desire and provocative of lust.
mn38:30.1: ‘On seeing a form with the eye, he lusts after it if it is pleasing; he has ill-will towards it if it is unpleasing; he abides with mindfulness of body unestablished and with limited cognizance[^5],
mn38:30.2: without understanding how the deliverance of the heart and the deliverance by understanding come to be, wherein those evil unprofitable dhammas cease without remainder.
mn38:30.3: Engaged as he is in favouring and opposing, when he feels any feeling, whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, he relishes that feeling, affirms it and remains cleaving to it.
mn38:30.4: When he does that, relishing arises in him.
mn38:30.5: Now relishing any of those feelings is clinging. With his clinging as condition, being; with being as condition, birth; with birth as condition, ageing and death have positive being, and (also) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.
mn38:30.6: That is how there is an origin to this whole mass of suffering.
mn38:30.7: On hearing a sound with the ear …
mn38:30.8: On smelling an odour with the nose …
mn38:30.9: On tasting a flavour with the tongue …
mn38:30.10: On touching a tangible with the body …
mn38:30.11: On cognizing a dhamma with the mind, he lusts after it if it is pleasing; he has ill-will towards it if it is unpleasing; he dwells with mindfulness of body unestablished and with limited cognizance,
mn38:30.12: without understanding how the deliverance of the heart and the deliverance by understanding come to be, wherein those evil unprofitable dhammas cease without remainder.
mn38:30.13: Engaged as he is in favouring and opposing, when he feels any feeling, whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, he relishes that feeling, affirms it and remains cleaving to it.
mn38:30.14: When he does that, relishing arises in him.
mn38:30.15: Now relishing any of these feelings is clinging. With his clinging as condition, being; with being as condition, birth; with birth as condition, ageing and death have positive being and (also) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.
mn38:30.16: That is how there is an origin to this whole mass of suffering.
mn38:31.1: ‘Here, bhikkhus, a Tathāgata appears in the world, Arahant and Fully Enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of men to be tamed, teacher of gods and men, enlightened, blessed.
mn38:31.2: He declares this world with its gods, its Māras and its Divinities, this generation with its monks and divines, with its kings and men, which he has himself realized by direct knowledge.
mn38:31.3: He teaches Dhamma good in the beginning, good in the middle and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing;
mn38:31.4: and he announces a life divine that is utterly perfect and pure.
mn38:32.1: A householder or householder’s son or one born in some clan hears that Dhamma.
mn38:32.2: On hearing the Dhamma he acquires faith in the Tathāgata.
mn38:32.3: Possessing that faith, he considers thus:
mn38:32.4: ‘House life is crowded and dirty; life gone forth is wide open.
mn38:32.5: It is not possible, living in a household, to lead a life divine as utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell.
mn38:32.6: Suppose I shaved off hair and beard, put on the yellow cloth, and went forth from the home life into homelessness?’
mn38:32.7: And on another occasion, abandoning perhaps a small, perhaps a large fortune, abandoning perhaps a small, perhaps a large circle of relatives, he shaves off hair and beard, puts on the yellow cloth, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
mn38:33.1: ‘Being thus gone forth and possessing the bhikkhus’ training and way of life, abandoning killing living beings, he becomes one who abstains from killing living beings, with rod and weapon laid aside, gentle and kindly, he abides compassionate to all beings.
mn38:33.2: Abandoning taking what is not given, he becomes one who abstains from taking what is not given, taking (only) what is given, expecting (only) what is given, he abides pure in himself by not stealing.
mn38:33.3: Abandoning what is not the life divine, he becomes one who lives the life divine, who lives apart abstaining from vulgar lechery.
mn38:33.4: Abandoning false speech, he becomes one who abstains from false speech, he speaks truth, cleaves to truth, is trustworthy, reliable and undeceiving of the world.
mn38:33.5: Abandoning malicious speech, he becomes one who abstains from malicious speech: as one who is neither a repeater elsewhere of what is heard here for the purpose of causing division from these, nor a repeater to these of what is heard elsewhere for the purpose of causing division from those, who is thus a reuniter of the divided, a promoter of friendships, and enjoying concord, rejoicing in concord, delighting in concord, he becomes a speaker of words that promote concord.
mn38:33.6: Abandoning harsh speech, he becomes one who abstains from harsh speech: he becomes a speaker of such words as are innocent, pleasing to the ear and lovable, as go to the heart, are civil, desired of many, and dear to many.
mn38:33.7: Abandoning gossip, he becomes one who abstains from gossip: as one who tells in season what is true and beneficial and the Dhamma and Discipline, he becomes a speaker of timely words, worth recalling, reasoned, measured and connected with good.
mn38:33.8: He becomes one who abstains from injuring seeds and plants.
mn38:33.9: He becomes one who eats in only one part of the day, refusing (food) at night and late meals.
mn38:33.10: He becomes one who abstains from dancing, singing, music and theatrical shows.
mn38:33.11: He becomes one who abstains from wearing of garlands, smartening with scent and embellishment with unguents.
mn38:33.12: He becomes one who abstains from high and large couches.
mn38:33.13: He becomes one who abstains from accepting gold and silver.
mn38:33.14: He becomes one who abstains from accepting raw corn.
mn38:33.15: He becomes one who abstains from accepting raw meat.
mn38:33.16: He becomes one who abstains from accepting women and girls.
mn38:33.17: He becomes one who abstains from accepting bondswomen and bondsmen.
mn38:33.18: He becomes one who abstains from accepting sheep and goats.
mn38:33.19: He becomes one who abstains from accepting poultry and pigs.
mn38:33.20: He becomes one who abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses and mares.
mn38:33.21: He becomes one who abstains from accepting fields and lands.
mn38:33.22: He becomes one who abstains from going on errands.
mn38:33.23: He becomes one who abstains from buying and selling.
mn38:33.24: He becomes one who abstains from false weights, false metal and false measures.
mn38:33.25: He becomes one who abstains from cheating, deceiving, defrauding and trickery.
mn38:33.26: He becomes one who abstains from wounding, murdering, binding, brigandage, plunder and violence.
mn38:34.1: He becomes one who is content with robes to keep the body, with alms-food to keep the belly: wherever he goes he takes all with him.
mn38:34.2: Just as wherever a winged bird flies it flies using its own wings,
mn38:34.3: so too he becomes one who is content with robes to keep the body, with alms-food to keep the belly: wherever he goes he takes all with him.
mn38:34.4: Possessing this store of Noble Ones’ virtue, he feels in himself pleasure that is blameless.
mn38:35.1: He becomes one who, on seeing a form with the eye, apprehends no signs and features
mn38:35.2: through which, if he left the eye faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade him. He practises the way of restraint, he guards the eye faculty, undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty.
mn38:35.3: On hearing a sound with the ear …
mn38:35.4: On smelling an odour with the nose …
mn38:35.5: On tasting a flavour with the tongue …
mn38:35.6: On touching a tangible with the body …
mn38:35.7: On cognizing a dhamma with the mind he apprehends no signs and features
mn38:35.8: through which, if he left the mind faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade him. He practises the way of restraint, he guards the mind faculty, undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty.
mn38:35.9: Possessing this Noble Ones’ faculty restraint, he feels in himself pleasure that is unadulterated.
mn38:36.1: He becomes one who acts in full awareness when moving forward and moving backward, who acts in full awareness when looking towards and looking away, who acts in full awareness when flexing and extending, who acts in full awareness when wearing the patched cloak, bowl and robes, who acts in full awareness when eating, drinking, chewing and tasting, who acts in full awareness when evacuating the bowels and making water, who acts in full awareness when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, talking and keeping silent.
mn38:37.1: He, possessing this store of the Noble Ones’ virtue, and possessing this Noble Ones’ contentment, and possessing this Noble Ones’ faculty restraint, and possessing this Noble Ones’ mindfulness and full awareness,
mn38:37.2: resorts to a secluded resting-place—to the forest, a tree-root, a rock, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a woodland solitude, an open space, a heap of straw.
mn38:38.1: On return from his alms-round after the meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, establishing mindfulness before him.
mn38:38.2: Abandoning covetousness for the world, he abides with a mind free from covetousness, he purifies mind from covetousness.
mn38:38.3: Abandoning ill-will and hatred, he abides without a mind of ill-will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings, he purifies mind from ill-will and hatred.
mn38:38.4: Abandoning lethargy and drowsiness, he abides with a mind free from lethargy and drowsiness, percipient of light, mindful and fully aware, he purifies mind from lethargy and drowsiness.
mn38:38.5: Abandoning agitation and worry, he abides unagitated with a mind stilled in himself, he purifies mind from agitation and worry.
mn38:38.6: Abandoning uncertainty, he abides with a mind crossed beyond uncertainty, unquestioning about profitable dhammas, he purifies mind from uncertainty.
mn38:39.1: Having thus abandoned these five hindrances, imperfections of mind that weaken understanding,
mn38:39.2: quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.
mn38:39.3: Again, bhikkhus, with the stilling of initial and sustained application, he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna …
mn38:39.5: and the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
mn38:40.1: ‘On seeing a form with the eye, he does not lust after it if it is pleasing; he has no ill-will towards it if it is not pleasing. He abides with mindfulness of body established and immeasurable cognizance[^6],
mn38:40.2: understanding how the deliverance of the heart and the deliverance by understanding come to be, wherein those evil unprofitable dhammas cease without remainder.
mn38:40.3: Having thus abandoned favouring and opposing, when he feels any feeling, whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, he does not relish that feeling, or affirm it, or remain cleaving to it.
mn38:40.4: When he does not do that, this relishing of those feelings ceases.
mn38:40.5: With cessation of his relishing (there is) cessation of clinging; with cessation of clinging, cessation of being; with cessation of being, cessation of birth; with cessation of birth, ageing and death cease, and (also) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.
mn38:40.6: That is how there is a cessation to this whole mass of suffering.
mn38:41.1: On hearing a sound with the ear …
mn38:41.2: On smelling an odour with the nose …
mn38:41.3: On tasting a flavour with the tongue …
mn38:41.4: On touching a tangible with the body …
mn38:41.5: On cognizing a dhamma with the mind, he does not lust after it if it is pleasing; he has no ill-will towards it if it is not pleasing. He abides with mindfulness of body established and immeasurable cognizance,
mn38:41.6: understanding how the deliverance of the heart and the deliverance by understanding come to be, wherein those evil unprofitable dhammas cease without remainder.
mn38:41.7: Having thus abandoned favouring and opposing, when he feels any feeling, whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, he does not relish that feeling, or affirm it, or remain cleaving to it.
mn38:41.8: When he does not do that, this relishing of those feelings ceases.
mn38:41.9: With cessation of his relishing (there is) cessation of clinging; with cessation of clinging, cessation of being; with cessation of being, cessation of birth; with cessation of birth, ageing and death cease, and (also) sorrow and lamentation, pain, grief and despair.
mn38:41.10: That is how there is a cessation to this whole mass of suffering.
mn38:41.11: ‘Bhikkhus, remember this Freedom due to craving’s Full Exhaustion (as taught) in brief by me. But the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, is caught up in a vast net of craving, in craving’s trammel.’
mn38:41.12: This is what the Blessed One said.
mn38:41.13: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
